How many counties does New York have, and who handles what?

New York has 62 counties. Five of them are the New York City boroughs: New York County (Manhattan), Kings (Brooklyn), Bronx, Richmond (Staten Island) and Queens. Those five have no official county seats. The other 57 counties have seats such as Mineola in Nassau County, Riverhead in Suffolk County and Canandaigua in Ontario County.

Below the county sit cities, towns and villages. That matters when you sell, because several different offices touch one house sale. Which office you deal with depends on where the property sits.

  • Assessor: sets the assessed value for your city or town, and hears questions about it.
  • County clerk: records the deed and receives the state transfer tax return for property outside New York City.
  • Tax receiver or treasurer: collects the bill. The name and the due dates change from one town or county to the next, so call the office on your tax bill.
  • Surrogate's Court: handles estates when the owner has died.

Who sets property tax in New York, and what is Grievance Day?

Property tax in New York is local. Your assessing unit values the house, and school districts, towns, villages and counties each add their levy. There is no single statewide due date, so a sale in Buffalo and a sale in Yonkers can look quite different at closing.

Grievance Day is the day you can challenge your assessment. Under Real Property Tax Law section 512, the board of assessment review begins hearing complaints on the fourth Tuesday of May, unless a city charter, county charter or special law sets another date. Units that share an assessor may pick a date as late as the second Tuesday of June.

Many owners also carry a STAR benefit on their school tax. Read our New York STAR exemption guide for the registration steps, and our New York property tax guide for liens and unpaid tax. Unpaid tax is normally paid from the sale proceeds at closing. If a lien has been sold or the house is headed to a tax sale, see tax deed and tax lien sales.

What taxes and fees come with selling a house in New York?

The seller pays the state real estate transfer tax. The rate is $2 for each $500 of consideration, which works out to 0.4 percent. For a one, two or three family house, the amount of any mortgage or lien that stays on the property is left out of the figure.

New York City adds a second layer. Inside a city of one million or more, an extra $1.25 per $500 applies when a residential conveyance is $3,000,000 or more. The city also has its own transfer tax. Our New York transfer tax guide lays out the state, city and local rates in one place.

The mansion tax is a separate 1 percent charge on residential sales of $1,000,000 or more. The buyer pays it, and the seller can become responsible if the buyer does not. See our mansion tax page.

How does recording a deed work in New York?

A deed is recorded with the clerk of the county where the property sits. Section 291 of the Real Property Law says an unrecorded conveyance is void against a later buyer who acts in good faith, pays value and records first. That is why recording happens right after closing and is not left for later.

For houses outside New York City, the transfer tax return, Form TP-584, goes to the county clerk, and the deed and tax are due by the 15th day after the deed is delivered. Inside the city, filings run through the city's own system, with different forms.

The same recording law has a consumer protection built in. After a residential conveyance is recorded, the clerk mails the owner of record a written notice that ownership documents were filed. If you ever receive one and did not sell, contact an attorney and the clerk right away.

Is foreclosure in New York judicial, and how long does it take?

Foreclosure in New York goes through the courts. The lender has to file a case, and a judge supervises the steps. We could not confirm a single typical timeline from an official page, because cases vary a great deal by county and by how the borrower responds.

Several protections apply to a home loan on a one to four family home that is the borrower's principal residence:

  • 90-day notice: Under RPAPL section 1304, the lender or servicer must mail a notice at least 90 days before starting the case. It must be in 14-point type and list free housing counselors.
  • Staying put: The notice states the borrower may remain in the home until a court orders otherwise. It is not an eviction notice.
  • Settlement conference: In a residential case where the defendant lives in the home, CPLR 3408 calls for a mandatory conference within 60 days after proof of service is filed with the county clerk.
  • Paying off the debt: Under RPAPL 1341, a defendant can stop the case by paying the amounts due into court, including principal, interest and costs.

If you are behind, a sale is one option. Talk with a housing counselor or an attorney first.

What happens when an owner dies and the house has to be sold?

New York decides who inherits when there is no will through Estates, Powers and Trusts Law section 4-1.1. With a spouse and children, the spouse takes $50,000 and half of what is left, and the children share the rest. With a spouse and no children, the spouse takes everything. With children and no spouse, the children take it all.

New York does have a small estate shortcut called voluntary administration, for estates with personal property of $50,000 or less. The same article says it does not apply to any interest in real property the person owned. In plain terms, a house usually cannot be handled through that shortcut, so expect to work with the Surrogate's Court in the county where the person lived.

An executor or administrator signs the deed, and the court paperwork has to be in order before a title company will insure the sale. Our New York probate guide goes through the steps.

What do sellers need to know about tenants and disclosures?

If tenants live in the house, a sale does not end their tenancy. Under Real Property Law section 226-c, a landlord who plans to raise rent by 5 percent or more, or not renew, must give written notice. The required notice is at least 30 days if the tenant has lived there less than a year, 60 days for one to two years, and 90 days beyond two years. The notice must also say whether the unit falls under the state's good cause eviction law. More is on our landlord and tenant page, and on squatters rights if someone is in the house with no lease.

On the seller side, Real Property Law section 462 asks the owner of a one to four family home to give the buyer a completed property condition disclosure statement before the buyer signs a binding contract. The form is based on what the seller actually knows and is not a warranty. It includes questions about floodplains and wetlands. The statute also says parties may still agree to an as-is sale of a home's physical condition.

Homeowners may also have a homestead exemption under CPLR 5206. The dollar cap depends on the county and is updated over time, so ask an attorney for the current figure.

What does a cash as-is sale mean in New York?

A cash as-is sale means the buyer takes the house in its present condition and does not need a mortgage. You do not paint, patch or replace anything, and there is no lender appraisal to wait on. The closing steps still apply: a title search, payoff of mortgages and liens, the transfer tax return, and recording of the deed.

We do not promise a price before we have seen the house. Tax dates, courts and clerks differ from place to place, so for anything we could not confirm on an official page, ask the county office.

Frequently asked questions

How many counties are in New York?

New York has 62 counties, including the five boroughs of New York City.

Who pays the transfer tax when I sell?

The seller pays the state transfer tax of $2 per $500. The buyer pays the 1 percent mansion tax on residential sales of $1,000,000 or more.

Where is my deed recorded?

With the clerk of the county where the property sits. Ask that office for current fees.

Is foreclosure handled by a court in New York?

Yes. It is a court process, and lenders must send a 90-day notice first on covered home loans.

Can I sell an inherited house without probate?

The small estate shortcut does not cover real property, so a house usually needs the Surrogate's Court. Ask the court in the right county.

Do I have to give the buyer a disclosure form?

Owners of one to four family homes must deliver a property condition disclosure statement before the buyer signs a contract.

When is Grievance Day?

Usually the fourth Tuesday of May, unless a charter or special law sets another date.

Do I need to fix the house first?

No. We buy as-is, so repairs and cleanouts are not required before you ask for an offer.
